title: a household's search answer leads to its missing entries one at a time
line: Ruth Peters's 1925 page alone is a household missing its head; FamilySearch's 1925 collection searched for Peters at Hempstead, Nassau, saved by hand, reaches her household's search by its own identity: it is page 1 of 6, so page 2 is the search's next save, and its rows are the candidates for the head, the five born too late to be her parent left out; Mary A Peters, whose name fits Mary Peters, whom the file names as Ruth's parent and so in the head's place, comes first whatever her birth year and is the one opened, and every row that fits nobody waits on the answer's pages; an earlier search of the same collection, surname and place, with the given name Mary, puts Mary Peters's row first, her record id differing from Ruth's in its last character alone; Mary's page saved for that candidate lands on page 19, line 23, the wife: the household regrouped holds her and Ruth and is still missing the head and line 24, the file's Mary is the wife held and no longer a name for the head, no row fits the file's Fredrick C Peters, and so no row is opened: the row born in 1887, the wife's year, stands first among the rows that fit nobody, and the answer's page 2 is the household's one open lead. No head's page is held, so the household is complete nowhere here

Ruth's plan written: her page alone is a household missing its head

expect.why: the household's search, under the household's own row and not her census row, which her own page holds: the first page of its answer, nothing of it held yet
